title: Notes
intro: Short interview notes live here. The knowledge base is grouped by topic so it can grow. The full conspect is on GitHub.

prep.title: Interview prep
prep.lead: About 100 spoken cards for a senior AQA interview: JavaScript, Git, CI, Playwright, frameworks, patterns, API, SQL, process. Filter a topic, open one question. Each answer names the term, then what I do with it. Code and tiny schemas where they help. To add a card: prep.groups[].items in notes-en.json and notes-uk.json, same id.

a: Event loop is the queue of JavaScript. The engine is single-thread for your code. It runs one thing at a time.
Order: all sync code first. Then microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask, code after await). Then macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval). Then again.
setTimeout(fn, 0) still runs last. Event loop is not a while loop.

items.q: Shallow copy vs deep copy of an object
a: Copy means a new object. Shallow copy copies only the first level. Nested objects stay the same reference. If I change nested.name, both objects see it.

Shallow: { ...user } or Object.assign({}, user). Deep copy copies the whole tree. I use structuredClone(user). JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(user)) also copies nested fields, but it drops functions, Date becomes a string, undefined is lost.
A Promise is an object for a value that comes later: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. .then() runs on success. .catch() runs on error.
async/await is the same Promise with easier syntax. await waits. try/catch handles the error. In Playwright almost every step is async. I always await click, expect, and API.
A closure is a function that remembers variables from the place where it was created, even after that outer function finished.
In tests I use a small factory: a function returns helpers that still know baseURL or userId.
These are array methods. They do not change the original array. They return a new value.
filter keeps items that pass a check. map turns each item into something new. reduce walks the list and builds one result, for example a count.
QA live coding is often this: keep failed tests, unique emails, count status codes.
=== is strict equal. Same value and same type. 1 === '1' is false.
== is loose equal. It converts types. 1 == '1' is true. In tests I use ===, also in Playwright expect when I compare a string and a number.
items.code:
1 === '1'  // false
1 == '1'   // true
null == undefined  // true
null === undefined // false

a: this is the object that owns the current call. In a normal function, this depends on how you call it. In an arrow function, this is taken from outside. Arrow does not make its own this.
In Playwright I rarely need this. In a page class I use this.page for the page of this object.
Scope is where a name is visible. var is function scope and can be used before the line (hoisting). let and const are block scope { }.
const cannot get a new assign. The object inside can still change. I use const by default, let when the value must change, I almost never use var.
Falsy values: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.
undefined means the value was not set. null means we set empty on purpose. I check res.body == null when the API may send nothing.
user?.email reads email only if user is not null or undefined. If user is missing, the result is undefined. No crash.
?? means: use the right side only if the left is null or undefined. 0 ?? 10 is 0. '' || 'x' would become 'x'. I use ?? for numbers that can be 0.
items.code: const email = user?.profile?.email ?? 'unknown';

a: JSON is a text format for data. stringify turns an object into a string. parse turns a string into an object.
I use it for API bodies and for logs. It is not a perfect deep clone: functions and undefined disappear.
items.code:
const body = JSON.stringify({ email: 'ada@test' });
const data = JSON.parse(body);

items.q: Promise.all vs await in a loop
a: await in a loop waits one by one. Slow if I have many independent calls.
Promise.all runs them together and waits for all. If one fails, all fail. For independent GETs I prefer Promise.all.

items.q: How I handle errors in async tests
a: try/catch around await. Playwright expect already throws if the assert fails. I do not swallow the error.
For API I check status first, then body. If the test should fail, I let it fail with a clear message.
typeof tells the primitive type: string, number, boolean, undefined, function, object. typeof null is 'object'. That is a JS quirk.
For lists I use Array.isArray(x). I use this when I check an API body: is items an array.
items.code:
Array.isArray(body.items)  // true for []
typeof null                 // 'object'

items.q: merge, rebase, fetch, pull, push — what each word means
a: Git is a tool that saves versions of files as commits. A commit is a snapshot with a message. A branch is a moving pointer to a commit. remote is the copy on the server (origin). origin/main is main on the server.
merge = join two branches. Git adds a merge commit with two parents. History stays as it happened.
rebase = take my commits and replay them on top of another branch. History looks like a straight line. I do not rebase a shared main.
fetch = download new commits from remote. My working files do not change.
pull = fetch + then merge (or rebase) into my branch. My files update.
push = send my local commits to remote so the team can see them.
items.code:
remote origin/main
    fetch ↓          ↑ push
local main / feature

pull  = fetch + merge (or rebase)
merge = extra merge commit, two parents
rebase = replay my commits on top, straight line

items.q: What is a branch and how I work with it
a: A branch is a name that points to a commit. git switch -c feat/login creates a new branch from where I am now.
I make a feature branch from updated main. I do not commit straight to main on a team project.
items.code:
git fetch origin
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c feat/login

a: A commit is a saved snapshot: files + author + message + parent. git add stages files. git commit -m 'message' saves the snapshot.
A good message says why, not only what. I do not put secrets in a commit.
A conflict means two commits changed the same lines. Git cannot choose. I open the file, keep the right code, git add, then git merge --continue or git rebase --continue.
I read locators and tests. I do not click accept all incoming.
items.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
getByTestId('save')
=======
getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })
>>>>>>> feat/login

a: git push --force overwrites the remote branch. The old commits on the server can disappear for others.
I never force push to main. If I must rewrite my own branch, I use --force-with-lease. It fails if someone else pushed first.
stash means put my unfinished changes on a shelf. The working tree becomes clean. Then I can switch branch.
git stash push -u saves. git stash pop brings the changes back. I stash only when I must change branch fast.
cherry-pick copies one commit onto my current branch. It does not bring the whole other branch.
I use it for a hot fix commit that must go to main without the rest of the feature.
items.code: git cherry-pick abc1234

a: git revert makes a new commit that undoes an old one. History stays. Safe on shared main.
git reset moves the branch pointer. --hard also drops files. I use reset only on my local branch that nobody pulled.
A pull request (PR) is a request to merge my branch into another branch, usually main. People review the diff. CI runs tests.
I do not merge if CI is red. I answer comments. Then squash or merge as the team wants.
.gitignore lists files Git should not track: node_modules, reports, .env. Secrets must not go to the repo.
If a file is already committed, adding it to gitignore is not enough. I must remove it from the index.
items.code:
node_modules/
test-results/
playwright-report/
.env

a: CI means Continuous Integration. Every push or PR runs checks automatically: install, tests, maybe lint. The team sees a red or green result.
CD means Continuous Delivery or Deploy. After green CI, the build can go to an environment. I am not the owner of production deploy. I own the test job in the pipeline.
items.code:
push / PR
  → checkout
  → install deps
  → lint / tsc  (quality gate)
  → tests
  → report + notify
  → merge only if green

a: A quality gate is a must-pass check in CI. If tests fail or lint fails, we do not merge. It is a rule, not a feeling that the product is good.
On my last project: tests on a PR to main, and a nightly job. No merge if the PR job is red.
Jenkins is a CI server. A Jenkinsfile is a text file in the repo that describes the pipeline: stages and steps.
Typical stages for tests: checkout (take code), install, run tests, publish report, notify chat. I can explain this flow. I do not claim I owned the whole Jenkins cluster.
GitHub Actions is CI inside GitHub. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows. A job is a machine run. A step is one command.
I used GitHub Actions for the public Playwright suite. For work CI I also used Jenkins. I do not claim GitLab CI as a strong commercial duty.
items.code:
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test

a: Static analysis reads code without running tests. ESLint finds style and bug patterns. tsc checks TypeScript types. Sonar is a platform some teams use.
Cursor is not static analysis. I use Cursor every day and I still read the diff. I did not run Sonar as a gate at work.

items.q: Tests pass local, fail in CI
a: I compare env, test data, time zone, browser version, workers. Local often has one worker and old cookies.
I open the CI trace or video. I do not start with waitForTimeout.
An artifact is a file CI keeps after the job: HTML report, trace, screenshot, video. Without it I cannot debug a red build.
I used Playwright HTML and Allure. The report is for the team, not only for me.
Retry means CI runs a failed test again. It can hide a flake. I use 1–2 retries in CI, zero local, so I still see the problem.
A flake that always needs retry is not green. I still open the trace and fix the wait or the data.
Sharding splits the suite across machines. --shard=1/3 runs the first third of files. Three jobs finish faster than one long job.
I know the idea. I used parallel workers on one machine more often than many shards.
items.code: npx playwright test --shard=1/3

a: A secret is a password or token. It lives in Jenkins credentials or GitHub Secrets, not in git.
Tests read it from env. I never print the token in the log.
npm ci installs exact versions from package-lock.json. It is for CI. Clean and repeatable.
npm install may update the lock file. I use npm ci in the pipeline.
PR job is short: smoke or a fast set, so review is not blocked for an hour.
Nightly is the full suite when people sleep. Both are CI. Quality gate for merge is the PR job.
Playwright is a tool to control a real browser from code. I write TypeScript tests. It can open Chromium, Firefox, WebKit.
It has a test runner with fixtures, locators, auto-wait, trace, and APIRequest. This is my main stack now.
Selenium talks to the browser through WebDriver. I used Java + Selenium at RIA.com. You often write extra waits.
Playwright talks to the browser more directly and waits for actionability for me. Today I choose Playwright for new UI work. I can still read Selenium code.
browser is the browser process (Chrome). context is one isolated profile, like incognito: cookies and storage are separate.
page is one tab inside a context. Parallel tests should not share one page. Playwright gives a fresh context/page per test by default.
items.code:
browser
  └─ context (cookies, storageState)
       └─ page (tab)
            └─ frame / locator

a: A Locator is a recipe how to find an element. It does not grab the node at create time. On each click it searches again. That is why it survives re-render.
ElementHandle is a snapshot of one node. It goes stale. I use locators, not page.$().
items.code: await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();

a: Order I like: getByRole, getByLabel, getByPlaceholder, getByTestId. Role means the accessible name a user and a screen reader see.
Long CSS and nth(3) break when the layout moves. data-testid is for automation. I still check it points to the real control.
items.code:
await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Email' }).fill(email);
await page.getByTestId('login-submit').click();

a: If a locator matches more than one node, Playwright throws. That is strict mode. It is good: I must make the locator unique.
I filter with .filter({ hasText }) or getByRole name. I do not hide the problem with .first() unless I can explain why.
Auto-wait: Playwright retries until the element is actionable — visible, enabled, stable — or until timeout.
waitForTimeout(5000) is sleep. It makes CI slow and flaky. I wait for a locator or waitForResponse instead.
expect(locator).toBeVisible() retries until true or timeout. It is not a one-shot check.
I assert the user result: button visible, text, URL. I do not assert only that click() did not throw.
items.code: await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Accounts' })).toBeVisible();

a: A fixture is setup and teardown that a test asks by name. Built-in: page, context, browser, request.
My fixtures go through test.extend. storageState is not a built-in fixture name. I save it after API login and reuse it.
test scope: new value for every test. Default for page. Isolated.
worker scope: one value for many tests in the worker. Good for a heavy login file. I do not put a shared page in worker scope.
storageState is a JSON of cookies and localStorage. After login I save it. Next tests start already logged in.
I usually login with API, then save storageState. A separate UI test still checks the login form.
items.code:
await request.post('/api/v1/auth/login', { data: { email, password } });
await page.context().storageState({ path: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' });

a: APIRequestContext sends HTTP without a browser. The request fixture is that client.
I use it for setup, teardown, and API checks. UI should not click login if API can create the session.
In the Northgate Console pet, in-browser REST is a Service Worker. There I wait with page.waitForResponse, not Playwright request.
page.route intercepts a network call in the browser. I can mock a JSON or fail the API on purpose.
I mock when the real service is slow or I need a rare error. I do not mock the happy path if I can hit a real test API.
I register waitForResponse before the click. Then I click. Then I assert status. Otherwise the call can finish before I listen.
This is how I catch 401 or 200 in the UI flow.
Trace is a recording of the test: DOM, network, steps. I open it with Playwright Trace Viewer.
On fail I look at the timeline, not only the log. Screenshot and video are extra artifacts in CI.
A frame is a page inside a page (iframe). I use page.frameLocator('iframe').getByRole(...).
A new tab is another page. I wait for popup with context.waitForEvent('page'), then work on that page.
This file is the runner config: baseURL, browsers (projects), retries, workers, reporter, timeout.
CI and local can differ: more retries in CI, one worker local when I debug.
A worker is a parallel process. Several tests run at the same time. Each test should have its own user or data.
If two tests edit the same account, they flake. I used different accounts for parallel runs.

items.q: How I run a subset of tests
a: I tag tests in the title: @smoke @api. Then npx playwright test --grep @smoke.
That is how a PR job stays short and nightly stays full.
playwright codegen records clicks. Cursor can draft a test. I never merge that blindly.
I rewrite locators, waits, and asserts. I own the test. AI is a draft.

items.q: How I structure a test project
a: A framework is the folder + rules, not only Playwright. Tests read as a flow. Details live in pages, fixtures, utils.
Typical: pages/, fixtures/, tests/ui, tests/api, utils/, playwright.config.ts. CI config sits next to the tests.
items.code:
tests/
  ui/
  api/
pages/
fixtures/
utils/
playwright.config.ts

a: Env means environment variables: baseURL, passwords. They live in .env or CI secrets, not in git.
A factory is a function that builds a user or an account. I do not copy the same JSON into five tests.

items.q: Playwright vs pytest vs Selenium in my career
a: Today I lead with TypeScript and Playwright. RIA.com: Java, Selenium, REST Assured. Clear Junction: Python, pytest, Selenium, Docker, later Playwright.
If the job is Python/pytest, I start with Clear Junction. I do not say pytest is my daily stack now.
TypeScript adds types on top of JavaScript. The editor and tsc catch a wrong field before CI.
Playwright ships types. I still write simple types, not clever generics.
Independent means test B does not need test A. I can run one file. Parallel does not break data.
Shared mutable user is the usual bug. I create data in beforeEach or via API, or I isolate users.
A tag is a label in the title: @smoke. The PR job runs smoke. Nightly runs all.
I do not put 200 UI tests on every PR if they take 40 minutes.
A reporter turns results into a page. Playwright HTML is built-in. Allure is another report some teams want.
I used both. The value is grouping fails: product vs flake vs data.

items.q: How I review AI-generated test code
a: Cursor drafts fast. I read locators, waits, test data, and the assert. If the assert does not hit a risk, I reject it.
I do not accept self-healing CSS. Role, label, test id stay my decision.
baseURL and users come from env: test, staging. The same tests, different data.
I do not hardcode https://prod inside a spec.
items.code:
const baseURL = process.env.BASE_URL;
expect(baseURL).toBeTruthy();

a: Test layer: the spec, the story. Page/API layer: how we click or call. Utils: wait helpers, dates. Config: env. Data: factories.
The spec should not new WebDriver or paste a 20-line fetch. That is what a senior interviewer wants to hear.
items.code:
spec → page object / api client → http + browser
         ↑ config + factories

a: POM is a pattern: one class per screen (or block). Locators and actions live there. The test calls login(), not fill('#x').
When the UI changes I edit one class. Limit: a giant page class is also bad. Then I split a component object.
AAA is a pattern for one test. Arrange = data and login. Act = one user action. Assert = one clear check.
I do not hide three unrelated asserts in a helper with no name.
The pyramid is a picture of volume. Bottom: many cheap unit and API tests. Top: few UI tests. UI is slow and flakes more.
I automate critical UI plus API. I do not cover every click with Playwright.
items.code:
UI (few, slow)
      API / integration
   unit (many, cheap)

a: These are access modifiers. They say who can see a field or method.

public = the test can call it. private = only this class (locators, helpers). protected = this class and a child class. Passwords are not a private field. Passwords live in env. In my Playwright pages I often keep locators private and actions public. I should not say everything is public.

items.q: Wait for a condition, not sleep
a: A condition wait means: until visible, until URL, until 200. Sleep means wait N ms no matter what.
Sleep hides races and comes back in CI.
A factory builds an object with defaults I can override. Each test can get a unique email.
Better than one shared user.json that parallel tests fight over.
items.code: const user = makeUser({ role: 'Admin' });

a: DRY means Do not Repeat Yourself. DAMP means Descriptive And Meaningful Phrases — the test should still read clearly.
If I hide the whole story in one mega-helper, the test is short and nobody knows what it checks. I repeat a little if it reads better.
When a widget is on many pages (header, modal), I extract a small class, not a 800-line page.
Same idea as POM, smaller scope.

items.q: Why I do not share one page across tests
a: A singleton browser for all tests was common in old Selenium. Tests leak cookies and order.
Playwright gives a new context per test. I keep that. Isolation first.

items.q: Screenplay pattern — do I use it?
a: Screenplay is actors + tasks + questions. Some teams like it for huge suites.
I do not have commercial Screenplay. I say POM + fixtures. If they use Screenplay, I can learn the names, I do not fake the experience.
API is a contract: the client sends HTTP, the server answers JSON (often). REST uses URLs for resources and HTTP methods for actions.
I test status, headers, body, and side effects in DB if I have access.
items.code:
GET    /accounts      read list
POST   /accounts      create
GET    /accounts/1    read one
PUT    /accounts/1    replace all fields
PATCH  /accounts/1    change some fields
DELETE /accounts/1    remove

items.q: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS
a: GET reads. It should not change data. POST creates or starts an action. DELETE removes.
HEAD is like GET without a body. OPTIONS asks which methods are allowed. I can name them. I use GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE every week.
PUT replace: I send the whole resource. Missing fields may become empty, depends on the API.
PATCH update: I send only fields to change. After both I check status and body.
2xx success: 200 OK, 201 created, 204 no body. 4xx my request is wrong: 400 validation, 401 no auth, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict.
5xx server error. I always assert the code, not only that the call did not throw.
401 Unauthorized: no valid auth. I am not in. 403 Forbidden: I am in, but this action is not allowed.
Token often goes in header Authorization: Bearer .... Cookie session lives in Cookie. I do not mix them in one test without a reason.
items.code:
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Cookie: session=...

a: Headers are metadata of the request or response: Content-Type, Authorization, Set-Cookie.
I check Content-Type is JSON when I expect JSON. I check the token is sent.
Schema means the shape of JSON: required keys and types. Status 200 is not enough if id is missing.
I did this in Postman. In code people often use Ajv. I do not claim Ajv as my daily work tool.
Idempotent means I can send the same request twice and the result stays the same. GET, PUT, DELETE should be. POST create often makes two rows.
I test double submit on pay or create if the product can duplicate.
Negative means I send bad input on purpose: empty body, wrong token, id that does not exist.
I expect 4xx, not 500, and a clear error field if the spec has one.
I create the account with POST, then open UI and see it. Faster and more stable than clicking the whole form every time.
I still keep one UI path for the form itself.

items.q: What is contract testing — my level
a: A contract is an agreement: this field exists, this type. Contract tests fail when producer and consumer drift.
I check schema in Postman/Playwright. I do not claim Pact as commercial experience.
Chain means I take id from POST and send it to GET or DELETE. I do not hardcode ids that die after a reset.
If POST fails, I stop. I do not call DELETE on undefined.

items.q: What is SQL for me as QA?
a: SQL is the language of relational databases: tables, rows, columns. I am not a DBA. I use SQL to check data, prepare test data, and compare API vs DB.
SELECT reads. WHERE filters. JOIN connects tables.
SELECT columns FROM table. WHERE keeps rows that match. =, <>, LIKE, IN.
I never SELECT * in a check if I need two fields. I know what I assert.
JOIN connects tables on a key. INNER JOIN keeps rows that match in both tables.
LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table. If there is no match, right columns are NULL. I use LEFT when I need accounts even without a transfer.
items.code:
accounts a
INNER JOIN transfers t ON t.from_id = a.id
  → only accounts that sent money

accounts a
LEFT JOIN transfers t ON t.from_id = a.id
  → all accounts, transfer columns may be NULL

a: GROUP BY buckets rows. COUNT, SUM, AVG run per bucket.
HAVING filters after the group. WHERE filters before. Example: statuses with more than 10 rows.
items.code:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM accounts
GROUP BY status
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

a: NULL means unknown / empty. NULL = NULL is not true. I use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
When I compare API and DB I remember: empty string is not NULL.
After POST I SELECT the row. If UI shows 100 and DB has 90, the bug is not only the button.
I map types: money, dates, status enums. I do not compare raw strings blindly.

items.q: What is an index — QA view
a: An index is a lookup structure. It makes WHERE faster. I do not design indexes.
If a report query is slow, I can mention missing index to a developer. I am not a DBA.
SQL injection is when user input becomes part of a query and changes it. Parameterized queries prevent it.
I am not a security tester. I can try a quote in a search field as a negative case. I do not claim a pentest.

items.q: Which story belongs to which job
a: RIA.com: only QA. Manual first. Then Java, Selenium, REST Assured. SQL and DB. Notifications from the database for managers.
Clear Junction: FinTech, Access and Identity. Python, pytest, Selenium, Docker. Later Playwright. I am not a payment-provider expert.
FRACTAL: first QA. Process, docs, regression, then Playwright UI plus API and Jenkins.
Strategy answers how we test: levels, tools, risks, what is in CI. Plan is closer to a concrete run: scope of this release, who, when.
On a new project I start with strategy: critical flows, API+UI, Jenkins. Then a shorter plan per sprint.
Shift-left means QA looks at the work earlier: comments on the ticket before code, examples, risks.
I did this: the ticket went to QA before development. Bad requirements did not wait until the end.
I spend more time where a fail is expensive: money, access, data. Payments, roles, freeze — more cases, more negatives.
A static page in one language gets smoke, not 40 UI tests.
EP = equivalence partition: one value stands for a group. BVA = boundary: 0, 1, max. Pairwise = every pair of parameters, not the full matrix.
Pairwise cuts the count and still hits combinations. I used pairwise-online for that.
I do not have a TMS number I can prove. I track critical flows in CI versus still manual versus too unstable to automate.
I should not say 90% if I cannot show how I counted.
I skip a flow that changes every week, a one-time check, and a case I cannot assert in CI.
Exploratory and the first look at a new screen stay manual first.

items.q: What is a flaky test and what I do
a: Flaky means pass and fail without a product change. Causes: wait, shared data, time, parallel.
I quarantine or skip only while I fix. I look at trace, network, isolation. Hard wait is not the first fix.

items.q: How I look for root cause
a: RCA means root cause analysis. I reproduce. Then logs, DevTools network, API body, DB.
I want the cause, not only a bug report. I ask a developer if I am stuck.
No process: I learn the product and docs, find the critical user flow, write the happy path, then negatives.
Then regression list, then automation and CI. Then a second QA can take manual while I stay on automation. This is FRACTAL.

sections.title: How I prepare
paragraphs: I refresh the stack I actually used: Playwright, API, SQL, CI, and how I explain the QA process.
I keep two versions of answers. Ukrainian is how I think. English is spoken: short sentences, one idea each, with real technical words (fixtures, storageState, 401).
I practice the story of the work, not only tool names: first QA on a project, what I automated and why, how I look for a root cause.

sections.title: What I am learning now
paragraphs: Interview prep is split by topic: JavaScript, Git, CI, Playwright, frameworks, patterns, API, SQL, process.
How to explain a framework and Jenkins jobs (merge request, branch, nightly) in a clear way.
Spoken English for work answers. My level is Upper-Intermediate. I say that honestly.
SQL and API checks for defect investigation.

sections.title: Playwright — short conspect
paragraphs: This is my main automation stack now: TypeScript and Playwright. I use it for UI, API (APIRequest), and end-to-end flows.
Framework shape I use: OOP, page objects, fixtures. Login is not repeated in every test when storageState can hold the session (cookies / auth).
I look at locators, frames, parallel runs, and flaky tests as part of the job, not as a surprise at the end.
I also used Java, Selenium, and Maven in commercial work at RIA.com. At Clear Junction and FRACTAL I used TypeScript and Playwright. Playwright is what I use today.

sections.title: What I automate
paragraphs: I automate flows that run often and must stay green in CI: regression, critical UI + API paths, repeated setup.
A useful automated test is one the team can trust after a merge.

sections.title: How I use Cursor
paragraphs: I use Cursor every day in automation work. It is a speed tool, not the owner of the test. I read every generated change before I merge: locators, waits, test data, and whether the assertion hits a real risk.

Refactoring: I use it to extract page objects, fixtures, and helpers, and to kill duplicated locators. The draft can come from the agent. I still check that the POM public API stays clear and that tests assert the same thing as before.

Debugging: I paste a Playwright trace, a CI log, a network call, or an API body and ask for hypotheses. I do not accept “add a wait” as a fix. I confirm the cause in DevTools, the API response, or SQL, then change the locator, the data, or the environment.

Ideas and artifacts: I brainstorm coverage gaps, negative API cases, and EP / BVA edges. I also get first drafts of test cases, checklists, bug reports, test-plan outlines, and RCA notes. I edit them before they go to the team.
Reports: from Allure or a Jenkins run I ask for a short failure grouping — flake vs product vs test data — then I write the note the team can act on.

How I keep it useful: project rules so new tests follow our POM and fixtures, not a generic Playwright sample. Boilerplate for a page, a fixture, APIRequest, or storageState is fine. I reject brittle CSS and “self-healing” locators. Stable roles, labels, and test ids stay my decision. I also turn a manual checklist into an automation outline, then I choose what is worth putting in CI.
